howtos.name: Holding a newborn
howtos.oneLiner: Picking up and holding a baby who feels too small.
howtos.when: From the first minute. The head and neck need your hand until bub can hold it up alone.
steps: Wash or sanitise your hands first, and ask visitors to do the same.
Slide one hand under their head and neck, and the other under their bottom.
Lift them slowly and bring them in against your chest in one smooth move.
Rest their head in the bend of your elbow with that forearm along their back.
Keep their chin up off their chest so their airway stays open.
Try them upright against your shoulder, with a hand spread across their back and neck.
Sit down before you pass them to someone else, and say out loud when you are letting go.
howtos.watchOut: Support the head and neck every single time, keep their chin off their chest, and never jiggle or shake a baby, however much you want the crying to stop.

howtos.name: Skin to skin
howtos.oneLiner: Bare chest cuddles that calm you both down.
howtos.when: Straight after birth, and any time in the first months. Partners and dads too.
steps: Take your top off, or open your shirt, and get comfortable somewhere with your back supported.
Strip bub down to their nappy and sit them upright against your bare chest.
Turn their head to one side so their face is clear and you can see it.
Lay a blanket over both of you, leaving their head and face uncovered.
Stay awake. Ask someone to sit with you if you are running on empty.
Give it twenty minutes or more, and let them feed if they start searching.
Move them to their own safe sleep space the moment you feel yourself drifting off.
howtos.watchOut: Skin to skin is for when you are awake and sitting up. Falling asleep with bub on your chest, especially on a couch or recliner, is not safe.

howtos.name: Breastfeeding attachment
howtos.oneLiner: Getting a deep latch so feeding does not hurt.
howtos.when: Every breastfeed, and especially if your nipples are sore or feeds feel like a fight.
steps: Get yourself comfortable first: back supported, shoulders down, a drink within reach.
Hold bub chest to chest with you, with their ear, shoulder and hip in one line.
Line their nose up with your nipple, not their mouth.
Brush their top lip with your nipple and wait for them to open wide, like a yawn.
Bring them in quickly, chin first, so the nipple goes in towards the roof of their mouth.
Check their chin is tucked in close, their bottom lip is rolled out, and you see more areola above than below.
Listen for swallowing, and look for a wide slow jaw movement rather than quick flicking.
If it pinches, break the suction with a clean finger in the corner of their mouth and start again.
howtos.watchOut: Pain is a signal, not the price of feeding. A deep latch feels like strong tugging, never pinching or biting. Ring the ABA helpline early.

howtos.name: Expressing and storing milk
howtos.oneLiner: Getting milk out by hand or pump, and storing it safely.
howtos.when: To build or keep up supply, to soften overfull breasts, or to leave milk for someone else.
steps: Wash your hands, and use parts and containers that have been washed and sterilised.
Get warm and comfortable, with bub nearby or a photo of them if they are not.
Soften things first with a warm cloth and some gentle breast massage.
By hand, cup your breast with thumb above and fingers below, back from the nipple, then press in, compress, release and repeat.
By pump, start on the lowest setting and only build up as far as stays comfortable.
Swap sides when the flow slows, then come back to each side again.
Label every container with the date, and get it into the fridge or freezer straight away.
Use the oldest milk first, and check the ABA storage times rather than guessing.
howtos.watchOut: Expressing should never hurt. Do not warm milk in the microwave, do not refreeze thawed milk, and tip out whatever bub leaves in a bottle.

howtos.name: Making up a bottle
howtos.oneLiner: Making up formula safely, one feed at a time.
howtos.when: Every formula feed. Make it fresh, and never save what is left over.
steps: Wipe the bench down, then wash and dry your hands.
Take a washed and sterilised bottle and teat out just before you need them.
Boil fresh tap water and let it cool as far as the tin's own directions tell you.
Pour the water into the bottle first, up to the mark you want.
Add the number of level scoops the tin's chart gives for that much water, never heaped or packed down.
Cap it and swirl or shake until there is no powder or lump left.
Cool it under a running cold tap, then test a drop on your inner wrist so it feels barely warm.
Feed it straight away, and tip out anything left at the end of the feed.
howtos.watchOut: Follow the tin, not a friend's recipe. Water in first, made fresh, never re-used, never microwaved, and never watered down or strengthened.

howtos.name: Giving a bottle
howtos.oneLiner: Feeding a bottle at bub's pace, with less wind.
howtos.when: Any bottle feed, of formula or expressed milk. Give it twenty to forty minutes.
steps: Test the temperature on your inner wrist. Barely warm, never hot.
Hold bub in your arm fairly upright, with their head higher than their tummy.
Brush the teat on their lips and wait for them to open and take it themselves.
Tilt the bottle just enough to keep the teat full of milk, rather than straight up.
Let them pause. Lower the bottle or slip the teat out for a moment when they stop sucking.
Stop about halfway to wind them, then offer the rest if they still want it.
Finish when they turn away, go floppy round the mouth or stop sucking, even with milk left.
Tip the rest out, then wash and sterilise everything for next time.
howtos.watchOut: Never prop a bottle or leave bub to feed alone, and never push the last few millilitres. A baby who turns away or goes limp around the mouth is finished.

howtos.name: Sterilising bottles and pump parts
howtos.oneLiner: Making bottles and pump parts safe to use again.
howtos.when: After every bottle or expressing session, for about the first twelve months.
steps: Rinse everything straight after the feed so milk does not dry on.
Pull every part off: teat, ring, cap, bottle, valves and membranes.
Wash in hot soapy water with a bottle brush, scrubbing inside the teat and around the threads.
Rinse in clean water and check there is no milk film left anywhere.
Sterilise by boiling, by steam, or with a chemical solution, following that method's instructions.
If you boil, keep everything fully under the water for five minutes with nothing poking out.
Leave the lid on until you need them, and lift them out with clean dry hands or tongs.
Put bottles together just before you make a feed, not hours ahead.
howtos.watchOut: Washing is not sterilising, and a sterile bottle handled with dirty hands is not sterile any more. Bin any teat that is cracked, cloudy or sticky.

howtos.name: Burping
howtos.oneLiner: Getting trapped air up so it stops hurting.
howtos.when: After a feed, and part way through if bub pulls off, squirms or cries mid feed.
steps: Sit up straight and put a cloth over your shoulder, because something will come up.
Hold bub upright against your chest with their chin resting past your shoulder.
Support their bottom with one hand and their head and neck with the other.
Rub slowly up their back, then pat with a cupped hand, firm but gentle.
Keep going for a minute or two, then try again with them sitting upright on your lap.
Lean them slightly forward with your hand under the chin and jaw, never across the throat.
Give up after about five minutes if nothing comes. Not every feed makes a burp.
howtos.watchOut: A burp is not compulsory. Patting harder and longer does not create one, and a baby folded forward at the neck cannot breathe properly.

howtos.name: Nappy change
howtos.oneLiner: A quick change with nothing escaping.
howtos.when: Around most feeds, and any time bub is dirty. Roughly six to ten times a day at first.
steps: Get everything within arm's reach first: nappy, wipes or warm water and cotton wool, cream, a bag.
Lay bub on a change mat on the floor, or on a change table with one hand always on them.
Undo the nappy, hold both ankles in one hand and lift their bottom gently.
Wipe front to back, fold the dirty nappy under them, then slide it out.
Clean and dry every crease, and let the skin air for a moment before the new nappy.
Slide the new nappy under, bring it up between their legs and tape it so one finger fits at the waist.
Fold the front down below the cord stump if it is still there, then wash your hands.
howtos.watchOut: Never turn away from a baby on a raised surface, not even for a second, and never leave them there alone. The floor is the safest change table you own.

howtos.name: Cleaning girls and boys
howtos.oneLiner: Cleaning a baby girl or boy the right way.
howtos.when: At every nappy change, and carefully after a dirty one.
steps: Use warm water and cotton wool, or fragrance free wipes, with plenty within reach.
For a girl, always wipe front to back so nothing travels forwards.
For a girl, clean the outer folds only. Do not open or clean inside the labia.
For a boy, wipe the whole area, including under the scrotum and into the groin creases.
For an uncircumcised boy, wash the outside of the penis only, and never pull the foreskin back.
Point the penis downwards inside the nappy before you tape it up.
Dry every crease, because damp skin is what turns into nappy rash.
howtos.watchOut: Never retract a baby boy's foreskin, and never clean inside a girl's labia. White discharge, or a little blood spotting in the first days, is normal in girls.

howtos.name: Cord care
howtos.oneLiner: Keeping the cord stump clean and dry until it drops off.
howtos.when: At every nappy change until the stump comes away, usually within one to two weeks.
steps: Wash your hands before you go near it.
Leave it alone as much as you can. Clean and dry beats fussing with it.
If it is dirty or sticky, wipe it with plain water and dry it gently.
Fold the front of the nappy down so it sits below the stump.
Let air get to it: loose clothing, and nothing with a tight band over the belly.
Expect it to dry out, darken and go crusty before it drops off by itself.
Never pull it off, even when it is hanging on by a thread.
howtos.watchOut: Ring your nurse or GP if the skin around it goes red, swollen, smelly or oozy, if it bleeds, or if bub has a fever or just seems unwell.

howtos.name: Topping and tailing
howtos.oneLiner: A quick wash of face, hands and bottom, no bath.
howtos.when: On the days between baths, or whenever a whole bath feels like too much.
steps: Fill a bowl with warm water and test it with your wrist or elbow.
Lay bub on a towel somewhere warm, with the heater on if the room is cool.
Wipe each eye with its own fresh piece of damp cotton wool, from the inner corner outwards.
Wipe the face, around and behind the ears, and into the folds of the neck, then pat dry.
Open each hand and wash the palm and between the fingers, then dry them.
Change the water, then clean the nappy area front to back and dry every crease.
Dress the top half first and get them covered up before they go cold.
howtos.watchOut: Fresh cotton wool for each eye so nothing travels from one to the other, and never poke inside their ears or nose. Outside only.

howtos.name: The first bath
howtos.oneLiner: The first proper bath, done calmly and safely.
howtos.when: Any time in the first week or two. There is no rush, and two or three baths a week is plenty.
steps: Warm the room, and lay the towel, nappy and clothes out before you start.
Fill the bath about ten centimetres deep, cold water in first and then hot, and swirl it through.
Test it with your elbow or inner wrist. It should feel barely warm, around thirty seven degrees.
Undress bub, leave the nappy on until the last second, and wrap them in the towel.
Lower them in feet first, their head and shoulders on your forearm and your hand holding the far armpit.
Wash with your free hand using water alone, or the smallest squeeze of plain baby wash.
Lift them straight onto the towel, wrap them up, and dry the neck folds and every crease.
Tip the water out as soon as you are finished.
howtos.watchOut: Never leave bub in the bath alone or with an older child, not even to grab a towel. Take them with you. Babies can drown in seconds in a few centimetres.

howtos.name: Cutting tiny nails
howtos.oneLiner: Trimming tiny nails without drawing blood.
howtos.when: Once scratches start appearing, usually weekly. Newborn nails are often too soft at first.
steps: Wait until bub is deeply asleep, or get someone else to hold and distract them.
Work in good light with baby nail scissors, baby clippers or an emery board.
Hold one finger at a time and press the fingertip pad down away from the nail.
Cut fingernails straight across in two or three small snips, not one big one.
Cut toenails straight across too, never curved down into the corners.
File any sharp edge smooth with the emery board.
If you nick the skin, press a clean cloth on it until it stops, then leave it alone.
howtos.watchOut: Do not bite their nails off and do not pull a loose nail away. If a fingertip goes red, swollen or weepy, get your nurse or GP to look at it.

howtos.name: Taking a temperature
howtos.oneLiner: Getting an actual number, not just a hot forehead.
howtos.when: When bub feels hot, is oddly sleepy or unsettled, or you are about to ring someone.
steps: Use a digital thermometer. Forget forehead strips and the back of your hand.
Read your thermometer's instructions, because under the arm and in the ear work differently.
Unwrap bub's top half and let them sit on your lap for a minute if they have been bundled up.
For under the arm, sit the tip in the middle of a dry armpit and hold their arm down against their side.
Wait for the beep, then write the number and the time down so you can tell someone.
Treat thirty eight degrees or more as a fever, and under three months old that means ringing someone today.
Ring 000 or go straight to hospital if they are floppy, very pale, breathing oddly or hard to wake.
howtos.watchOut: A fever in a baby under three months always needs a doctor the same day, even if they seem fine. Never work out a medicine amount yourself. Ask.

howtos.name: Tummy time
howtos.oneLiner: Awake, watched time on the front to build strength.
howtos.when: From the first week, whenever bub is awake and alert. Never for sleeping.
steps: Pick a moment when they are awake and calm, not straight after a feed.
Clear a firm flat space, a play mat or a rug on the floor.
Lay them on their tummy with their head turned to one side and their arms forward.
Get down on the floor face to face and talk to them, because your face is the whole point.
Start with one or two minutes, two or three times a day, and build up from there.
Try it across your lap or on your chest instead if the floor is a hard no at first.
Pick them up when the grizzling starts, before it becomes a meltdown.
howtos.watchOut: Stay right beside them the whole time, and never let tummy time turn into a nap. If they drop off, move them onto their back in the cot.

howtos.name: Swaddling
howtos.oneLiner: Wrapping with arms down and hips free, the Red Nose way.
howtos.when: For sleeps in the early weeks, if it settles them. Stop at the first sign of rolling.
steps: Lay a lightweight cotton or muslin wrap out flat and fold the top corner down a hand's width.
Put bub on their back with their shoulders just below the fold.
Bring one side across their chest, that arm down beside their body, and tuck the end under them.
Bring the other side across the same way, firm enough to stay put but not tight.
Leave the wrap loose from the hips down so their legs can bend up and spread out.
Check you can slide a flat hand between the wrap and their chest.
Keep the wrap below their shoulders and well away from the face and head.
Stop wrapping altogether as soon as there is any sign of rolling, often around four to six months.
howtos.watchOut: Firm but not tight, arms down, hips free to bend and spread, nothing over the face. A wrapped baby always sleeps on their back, and wrapping stops at rolling.

howtos.name: Dressing for sleep
howtos.oneLiner: Dressing bub for the room, not for the forecast.
howtos.when: Every sleep. Go by the temperature of the room rather than the weather outside.
steps: Dress bub in about what you are comfortable in, plus one light layer.
Start with a singlet and a cotton sleepsuit, then add or drop layers from there.
Use a safe infant sleeping bag with a fitted neck and armholes, and no hood.
If you use blankets instead, lay bub on their back with their feet near the bottom end of the cot.
Tuck light blankets in firmly, no higher than their chest, with their arms out over the top.
Skip hats, beanies and hoods indoors, because babies lose heat through their head.
Feel the back of their neck or their chest. Warm is right, clammy or sweaty is too hot.
When you are unsure, take a layer off rather than adding one.
howtos.watchOut: Overheating is the risk, not cold. No quilts, doonas, pillows, cot bumpers or soft toys in the cot, and nothing that could end up over the face.

howtos.name: Settling and resettling
howtos.oneLiner: Calming a newborn, and resettling them when they wake.
howtos.when: At the start of a sleep, or when they wake and grizzle twenty to forty minutes in.
steps: Watch for the tired signs first: jerky arms, grizzling, staring past you, yawning.
Dim the lights, cut the noise, and keep your own voice low and boring.
Run through the simple things: hungry, wet, too hot, too cold, wants you.
Hold them against your chest and sway or rock gently, or try a slow shush.
Put them in the cot on their back while they are drowsy but still awake if you can manage it.
Give them a few minutes to grumble their way back down before you lift them again.
If it turns into real crying, pick them up and start the whole thing again.
howtos.watchOut: You cannot spoil a newborn by cuddling them, but you can wear yourself out. If the crying is relentless and nothing helps, ring your MCH nurse.

howtos.name: Into the cot, not onto you
howtos.oneLiner: Moving a sleeping baby off you and into the cot.
howtos.when: When you want your arms back, and for every sleep you can manage it.
steps: Get the cot ready first: firm flat mattress, fitted sheet, nothing else in there.
Wait until they go properly floppy, often ten to twenty minutes after they drop off.
Keep one hand firmly on their back and bottom as you stand up and turn.
Lower them bottom first, then shoulders, and let their head settle last.
Leave your hands resting on them for a slow count of twenty before you lift them away.
If they stir, put a hand on their chest or shush quietly instead of picking them up.
Try putting them down drowsy but awake sometimes, so the cot stops being a surprise.
If it falls apart, pick them up and try again next sleep. It takes practice for both of you.
howtos.watchOut: They go down on their back in their own cot every time, on a firm flat mattress, with nothing loose in there and their face left uncovered.

howtos.name: The night feed
howtos.oneLiner: Feeding at 2am without waking everyone right up.
howtos.when: Every night feed for the first few months. Newborns are meant to feed overnight.
steps: Set up before bed: a drink and a snack for you, nappies, wipes, a spare wrap, a muslin.
Leave one dim lamp or a night light on and the big light off.
Change the nappy first only if it is dirty or soaked, otherwise feed first.
Feed somewhere you will not doze off with bub on you, propped up in bed or a firm chair.
Keep it dull. No chatting, no playing, no phone screen lighting up their face.
Wind them, and change them only if you have to.
Put them back in their own cot, on their back, and tuck any blanket no higher than their chest.
Get yourself back into bed, even if you feel wide awake.
howtos.watchOut: Falling asleep with bub on a couch or armchair is the real danger. If you might nod off, feed in bed and put them back in their cot before you sleep.

howtos.name: Using a dummy
howtos.oneLiner: Using a dummy without letting it take over.
howtos.when: Once feeding is going well, usually after the first few weeks, if you decide to use one.
steps: Decide together. A dummy is a tool, not a failure, and plenty of babies never take one.
If you are breastfeeding, wait until feeding is established before you offer one.
Offer it at the start of a sleep, after a feed, when you know they are not hungry.
Sterilise it before the first use and wash it often after that.
Never dip it in anything sweet, and never tie it to bub, their clothes or the cot.
If it falls out once they are asleep, leave it out.
Check it often for cracks, stickiness or a stretched teat, and replace it then.
howtos.watchOut: Never attach a dummy to a cord, ribbon or clip anywhere near sleep, and never use one to push a feed back. It is for settling, not instead of feeding.

howtos.name: Car seat basics
howtos.oneLiner: Getting bub home safely in a rearward facing seat.
howtos.when: Sort it before the birth. You cannot bring bub home without one fitted properly.
steps: Buy or hire a seat that meets the Australian standard and carries the sticker to prove it.
Choose a seat that suits your baby's size now, not the one they will grow into.
Fit it rearward facing, and keep it rearward facing for as long as bub still fits it that way.
Read that seat's own manual and follow it, because every model is different.
Book a professional fitting check. Councils, hospitals and motoring clubs do them.
Every trip, do the harness up so the straps lie flat, sit snug and come from the right height.
Check you cannot pinch a fold of webbing at their shoulder, and keep bulky jackets out of the harness.
Keep early trips short, and do not use the capsule as a bed once you are home.
howtos.watchOut: A capsule is for travelling, not for sleeping in at home. Get the fit checked by someone trained rather than trusting how tight it feels to you.

howtos.name: The night shift, as a team
howtos.oneLiner: Splitting the nights so one of you sleeps properly.
howtos.when: From the first night home. Agree the plan before you are both wrecked.
steps: Talk it through in daylight, not at 3am when you are both raw.
Split the night into two blocks so each of you gets one solid unbroken stretch.
Whoever is off duty sleeps somewhere else, with earplugs, and does not get up.
If you are breastfeeding, the other one does the change, the wind and the resettle.
If bottles are in the mix, swap whole feeds so you each get a real break.
Log feeds and sleeps in the app instead of trying to remember them in the morning.
Swap who gets the first block regularly, and take turns on the rough nights.
Review it every week or so, because bub keeps changing the rules.
howtos.watchOut: Exhaustion is not a competition, and saying you are at the end is not weakness. If either of you is not coping, ring your MCH nurse or a parent helpline.
